newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to lift ban on workers' May Day parade.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to lift ban on workers' May Day parade.

text.p: Mexico's most powerful union leader on Monday said pro-government workers would be allowed to march in this year's May Day parade, overturning a two-year ban imposed because of fears of unrest.
But in comments that implied that friction in the labour movement still ran deep, Fidel Velazquez, the 96-year-old patriarch of the powerful Labor Congress, hit out at a rival union leader.
Radio Red quoted Velazquez as saying that telephone workers' leader Francisco Hernandez was only fit to set up a rival union umbrella group if "he informs the public why he is a homosexual".

Hernandez and other independent labour leaders have mulled setting up a union to rival the Labor Congress, describing it as anti-democratic and out of touch with worker demands in a country where real wages have fallen sharply in the past two decades.

Hernandez denied he was a homosexual, but added that sexual preferences were unimportant. "It may be a question of age, I don't know," he said. "But it seems to me that to stoop to personal insults is an excess.
"The Labor Congress now has no remedy. It's an organisation that has weakened, it has lost all its value," he said.

Velazquez's control of the labour movement, that he has led with unswerving loyalty to the government for more than half a century, has been undermined since 1994 by a devaluation that plunged Mexico into its worst economic crisis in 50 years.

Shortly afterwards, he agreed to scrap the May Day march after fears that workers, angry over the crisis, would turn violent. On Monday, he said the march would be permitted this year because the economy was on the mend.
But the recovery may have come too late to save Velazquez's fortunes. On Monday, the Universal newspaper ran a poll saying some 90 percent of Mexicans believed he should retire.
